lead: Electronic fuel control works out the air entering the engine, computes the fuel mass that air needs, and holds each injector open for the time that delivers it. An exhaust oxygen sensor reports what actually burned, and the ECU trims the pulse to keep λ = 1. Every petrol car sold under today's emission norms runs this loop.
prereq: You need: open and closed loop from concept of electronic engine control. The sensors (manifold absolute pressure, air flow, throttle, temperature and oxygen) and the stepper and solenoid actuators are covered under Automotive sensors and actuators.

sections.h3: From the carburettor to petrol injection

blocks.text: A carburettor speeds the incoming air through a narrow throat, the venturi; the pressure drop there draws fuel through a fixed jet. Nothing measures the result, so on a hot afternoon, a cold start or a sudden throttle opening the mixture drifts away from the ratio the catalyst needs. The emission norms tighten that ratio at every stage.

Electronic control of carburetion was the stop-gap: a solenoid valve bled air into the carburettor fuel circuits, moved by the ECU from the oxygen-sensor signal. It held λ near 1 at steady cruise, but cold starts, transients and the uneven split of mixture between cylinders stayed poor.

Petrol injection replaced the jet with a solenoid valve opened for a computed time. An electric pump in the tank sends fuel through a filter to a fuel rail; a pressure regulator holds the rail about 3 to 4 bar above the manifold pressure for port injection, so the flow depends only on open time.

items: Throttle-body (single-point) injection: one or two injectors above the throttle. Cheap, but slow on transients and uneven between cylinders.
Port (multi-point) fuel injection: one injector per cylinder in the intake port, sprayed at the back of the intake valve. The common layout.
Gasoline direct injection: the injector sprays into the cylinder at about 50 to 200 bar. It cools the charge and allows stratified lean running, but makes more fine particles.

blocks.text: Port injectors can fire all at once once per revolution (simultaneous), in two groups (group), or each just before its own intake stroke (sequential, which needs a camshaft sensor to know the cylinder). Sequential gives the best emissions.

sections.h3: The injector and the fuel calculation

blocks.text: Inside the injector a coil pulls an armature and needle off its seat against a spring; fuel at rail pressure sprays through the nozzle. When the current stops the spring closes the needle. The static flow is the fuel the injector passes when held fully open, quoted at a stated pressure. Because the needle takes a fraction of a millisecond to open, the ECU adds a dead time (about 0.5 to 1 ms, longer at low battery voltage) to every pulse.

items: Saturated drive: battery voltage across a high-resistance coil (about 12 to 16 Ω) for the whole pulse. Simple and cheap.
Peak-and-hold drive: for a low-resistance coil, a high current (about 4 A) opens the needle fast, then the driver drops to about 1 A to hold it. Faster opening, cooler coil.

blocks.text: The speed-density calculation turns manifold pressure into an open time in four steps.

items: Air density from manifold absolute pressure p and intake temperature T: ρ = p ÷ (R T), with R = 287 J/(kg·K).
Air mass flow: ṁ<sub>air</sub> = η<sub>v</sub> × ρ × V<sub>d</sub> × N ÷ 2.
Fuel per injection: (ṁ<sub>air</sub> ÷ AFR) ÷ (injections per second).
Open time = fuel per injection ÷ injector flow, plus the dead time.

blocks.text: Here η<sub>v</sub> is volumetric efficiency, the air actually trapped divided by the swept volume's worth at manifold density, read from a map (typically 0.8 to 0.9 at full load; tuned intakes can push it slightly above 1). V<sub>d</sub> is the total swept volume in m³, N is speed in rev/s, and ÷ 2 is because a four-stroke fills each cylinder once every two revolutions. AFR is 14.7 at λ = 1. Engines with a hot-film mass airflow (MAF) sensor skip the first two steps: they read ṁ<sub>air</sub> directly.
The base pulse is then corrected: extra fuel when the coolant is cold, a short extra pulse when the throttle opens suddenly (fuel wets the port walls), and a longer dead time at low battery voltage.

sections.h3: Closed loop, fuel trim and the actuators

blocks.text: The switching oxygen sensor says only rich (high voltage) or lean (low voltage), not by how much. So the ECU ramps the pulse leaner until the sensor flips lean, then ramps richer until it flips rich, and so on: the mixture hunts around λ = 1 about once or twice a second. That hunt suits the catalyst, which stores a little oxygen on lean swings and releases it on rich swings.

Short-term fuel trim (STFT) is that live correction, a percentage added to or taken from the base pulse. When STFT stays biased one way, the ECU learns the offset into a long-term fuel trim (LTFT) table against speed and load, so the next start begins from the corrected value. LTFT hides slow drift, such as a dirty air-flow sensor or a weak pump, until it reaches its limit and sets a fault code.

items: EGR valve: a stepper motor, or a vacuum diaphragm switched by a solenoid, opens a passage from exhaust to intake to cut NOx.
Idle air stepper motor: a pintle moves to bypass air around the closed throttle, setting idle speed when cold or loaded by the air-conditioner or alternator.
EVAP purge solenoid: opens to draw petrol vapour from the charcoal canister into the intake. That vapour is extra fuel, so the sensor reads rich and the ECU shortens the injector pulse to keep λ = 1.

examples.question: A four-cylinder 1.6 L petrol engine with sequential port injection runs at 3000 rpm at full throttle. The manifold absolute pressure is 100 kPa, intake air is at 27 °C and volumetric efficiency is 0.85. The air-fuel ratio is 14.7:1. Each injector flows 3.0 g/s when fully open, and the dead time is 0.9 ms. Find the air mass flow, the fuel per injection, the commanded pulse width and the injector duty.
steps: Air density ρ = p ÷ (RT) = 100 000 ÷ (287 × 300) = 1.161 kg/m³; take 1.16 kg/m³.
N = 3000 ÷ 60 = 50 rev/s. Swept volume filled per second = V<sub>d</sub> × N ÷ 2 = 0.0016 × 25 = 0.040 m³/s.
Each injector fires once per cycle: 25 times a second, so 4 × 25 = 100 injections a second. Fuel per injection = 2.683 ÷ 100 = 0.02683 g = 26.83 mg.
Open time for that fuel = 0.02683 ÷ 3.0 = 0.00894 s = 8.94 ms. Commanded pulse = 8.94 + 0.9 = 9.84 ms.
examples.answer: Air flow 39.44 g/s, fuel 26.83 mg per injection, commanded pulse 9.84 ms (8.94 ms of flow plus 0.9 ms dead time), duty 24.6 %.

rho = 100e3/(287*300)
print(round(rho, 3))
air = 0.85*1.16*0.0016*25*1000
print(round(air, 2))
mg = air/14.7/100*1000
print(round(mg, 2))
t = mg/1000/3.0*1000
print(round(t, 2)); print(round(t + 0.9, 2)); print(round((t + 0.9)/40*100, 1))

traps: Using the full swept volume every revolution: a four-stroke fills each cylinder once every two revolutions, so use V<sub>d</sub> × N ÷ 2.
Using an ambient density at part throttle: speed density needs the manifold density from MAP and intake temperature.
Confusing milliseconds with milligrams: pulse width is a time, fuel per injection is a mass; the injector flow converts one into the other.
Forgetting the dead time: the commanded pulse is the flow time plus the opening delay.
Thinking the oxygen sensor sets the mixture: it only trims a base pulse from the map, and it is cold and ignored at start-up.

quiz.q: State the stoichiometric air-fuel ratio of petrol and what λ = 1 means.
quiz.a: 14.7:1 by mass. λ = 1 means the actual air-fuel ratio equals this value.

quiz.q: Why can a carburettor not hold λ = 1 across all speeds and loads?
quiz.a: Its jets are fixed holes, so the fuel follows the venturi pressure drop, not a measured air mass. Air density, temperature and transients shift the mixture, and nothing feeds back from the exhaust.

quiz.q: Distinguish short-term and long-term fuel trim.
quiz.a: STFT is the live percentage correction while the ECU hunts around λ = 1. LTFT is the learned offset stored against speed and load, used as the new starting point for wear or drift.

quiz.q: An engine takes 30 g/s of air at 14.7:1. Four injectors each fire 40 times a second and each flows 2.5 g/s. Find the flow time per injection.
quiz.a: Fuel = 30 ÷ 14.7 = 2.041 g/s. Injections = 4 × 40 = 160 per s. Fuel per injection = 12.76 mg. Time = 0.01276 ÷ 2.5 = 5.10 ms (add the dead time for the commanded pulse).

quiz.q: On an engine with a mass airflow sensor, long-term trim reads +18 % at idle but only +2 % at cruise. What single fault explains this?
quiz.a: Air leaking in after the air-flow sensor (a split hose or a leaking manifold gasket). The leak is unmetered, so the mixture runs lean. At idle the metered air is small and the leak is a large share of it; at cruise it is a small share, so the trim is small.

quiz.q: Name the two injector drive methods and one advantage of each.
quiz.a: Saturated drive: simple, cheap driver. Peak-and-hold: the needle opens faster and the coil runs cooler.

quiz.q: Manifold pressure is 60 kPa and intake air is at 30 °C. Find the manifold air density.

beyond: Not for the exam. Many new engines combine port and direct injectors to keep particles low while still cooling the charge, and gasoline particulate filters meet the latest particle limits. Model-based air estimation replaces the steady volumetric-efficiency map with a filling-and-emptying model of the manifold. Wideband lambda sensors give a measured λ instead of a rich-or-lean answer. Search next for "gasoline particulate filter", "wideband lambda sensor" and "wall wetting compensation".
